lesson_blocks.title: Learning Objective
lesson_blocks.content: By the end of this lesson, the learner should be able to explain Artificial Intelligence in simple language.

lesson_blocks.title: What Does AI Mean?
lesson_blocks.content: AI stands for Artificial Intelligence. Artificial Intelligence refers to computer systems designed to perform certain tasks that normally involve abilities associated with human intelligence. These tasks can include understanding language, recognizing images, recognizing speech, finding patterns, generating content, making recommendations, making predictions, and helping solve problems among others.

lesson_blocks.title: Simple Example
lesson_blocks.content: A learner asks Generative AI (GEN AI): "Explain photosynthesis to a 10-year-old." An AI system can interpret the instruction and generate a simple explanation. That is an example of Artificial Intelligence working with language.

lesson_blocks.title: Activity 1
lesson_blocks.content: What does AI stand for?

lesson_blocks.title: Activity 2

lesson_blocks.title: Activity 3

lesson_blocks.title: AI in Everyday Life
lesson_blocks.content: Many people already interact with AI without realizing it.

lesson_blocks.title: Smartphones
lesson_blocks.content: AI may be used for voice recognition, predictive typing, image enhancement, translation, and facial recognition.

lesson_blocks.title: Email
lesson_blocks.content: AI may be used for spam detection, message categorization, writing suggestions, and fraud or phishing detection.

lesson_blocks.title: Maps

lesson_blocks.title: Online Shopping

lesson_blocks.title: Social Media
lesson_blocks.content: AI may be used to recommend videos, posts, music, and accounts.

lesson_blocks.title: Banking
lesson_blocks.content: AI may be used for fraud detection, risk assessment, customer support, and pattern recognition.

lesson_blocks.content: Give five examples of places where AI may be used.

episodes.title: AI Is Not a Human
episodes.description: AI can produce impressive results, but AI is not automatically correct and can make mistakes.

lesson_blocks.title: AI Is Not a Human
lesson_blocks.content: AI can produce impressive results. However, AI is not automatically correct, a human expert, an unbiased and reliable source for every claim, or able to understand every situation perfectly. AI can make mistakes.

lesson_blocks.title: Foundation Rule
lesson_blocks.content: ASK → REVIEW → VERIFY → USE

lesson_blocks.title: Can AI sound confident and still be wrong?
lesson_blocks.content: Yes.

lesson_blocks.title: Does a professional-sounding AI response prove that the information is correct?
lesson_blocks.content: No.

lesson_blocks.title: Why is human judgment still important?
lesson_blocks.content: Because AI may misunderstand context, generate incorrect information, omit important details, or make unsuitable recommendations.

episodes.title: Basic AI Terminology
episodes.description: Learn the basic terms used when discussing Artificial Intelligence, automation, assistants, and agents.

lesson_blocks.title: Artificial Intelligence
lesson_blocks.content: Technology designed to perform certain tasks associated with human intelligence.

lesson_blocks.title: Machine Learning
lesson_blocks.content: Methods that allow computer systems to learn patterns from data.

lesson_blocks.title: Generative AI
lesson_blocks.content: AI capable of generating new content.

lesson_blocks.title: Model
lesson_blocks.content: A trained computational system that processes inputs and produces outputs.

lesson_blocks.title: Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: An instruction, question, or input provided to an AI system.

lesson_blocks.title: Output
lesson_blocks.content: What the AI system produces.

lesson_blocks.title: Data
lesson_blocks.content: Information used by computer systems.

lesson_blocks.title: Automation
lesson_blocks.content: Using technology to perform defined tasks automatically or with reduced manual effort.

lesson_blocks.title: Workflow
lesson_blocks.content: A sequence of steps used to complete a task or process.

lesson_blocks.title: AI Assistant
lesson_blocks.content: An AI-powered system designed to help users with particular tasks or information.

lesson_blocks.title: AI Agent
lesson_blocks.content: At a foundation level, an AI-powered system that can work through multiple steps toward a defined goal and potentially interact with approved tools.

title: Generative AI and Prompting
description: Learn what Generative AI is, how to communicate with AI using prompts, how to structure stronger instructions, and how to improve AI responses through iteration.

episodes.title: What Is Generative AI?
episodes.description: Understand what Generative AI is, how it differs from the broader concept of Artificial Intelligence, and the types of content it can create.

lesson_blocks.title: What Is Generative AI?
lesson_blocks.content: Generative AI is the branch of Artificial Intelligence that can create new content based on instructions or input provided by a user. It can generate text, images, audio, video, computer code, and other types of content.

lesson_blocks.title: How Generative AI Fits Into Artificial Intelligence
lesson_blocks.content: Artificial Intelligence is the broader field. It includes systems that can recognize patterns, make predictions, classify information, recommend items, understand language, and perform many other tasks. Generative AI is one part of this broader field. Its distinguishing capability is that it can generate new content in response to an instruction or other input.

lesson_blocks.title: What Does Generate Mean?
lesson_blocks.content: To generate means to produce or create an output. For example, when you ask a Generative AI system to write an email, explain a topic, create an image, summarize notes, or produce computer code, the system generates a new response based on your request and the patterns it learned during training.

lesson_blocks.title: What Can Generative AI Create?
lesson_blocks.content:
Generative AI can produce many kinds of output, including:

Text — explanations, emails, reports, stories, summaries, and ideas.

Images — illustrations, concepts, and other visual content.

Audio — generated speech, sounds, and other audio content.

Video — generated or transformed video content.

Computer code — code examples, explanations, and suggestions for programming tasks.

The exact capabilities depend on the AI system being used.

lesson_blocks.title: Example Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Write a short welcome message for new students.

lesson_blocks.title: Possible Output
lesson_blocks.content: Welcome to your AI learning journey. This course will guide you from the basics of Artificial Intelligence to practical AI problem-solving.

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Example
lesson_blocks.content: In this example, the learner provides an instruction asking the AI to write something. The AI interprets the request and generates new text as its output. This is a simple example of Generative AI working with language.

lesson_blocks.title: Check Your Understanding
lesson_blocks.content: If you ask AI to write a poem, which AI capability are you using?

episodes.title: What Is a Prompt?
episodes.description: Learn what a prompt is and understand how adding context, detail, and clear instructions can improve the response produced by Generative AI.

lesson_blocks.title: What Is a Prompt?
lesson_blocks.content: A prompt is an instruction, question, or other input that you give to an AI system to communicate what you want it to do. When using Generative AI, the prompt helps guide the response the AI produces.

lesson_blocks.title: Why Prompts Matter
lesson_blocks.content: Generative AI cannot automatically know exactly what you have in mind. It works from the information and instructions you provide. A vague prompt may produce a broad or less useful response, while a clearer prompt gives the AI more information about the task, context, level of detail, and type of answer you need. This does not guarantee that the response will always be correct, but it can make the output more relevant to your goal.

lesson_blocks.title: From Weak to Stronger Prompts
lesson_blocks.content: A prompt can be very simple or highly detailed. As a beginner, one useful way to understand prompting is to compare a weak prompt, a better prompt, and a stronger prompt. Notice how each version gives the AI more useful direction.

lesson_blocks.title: Weak Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Business.

lesson_blocks.title: Why This Prompt Is Weak
lesson_blocks.content: The word "Business" is too broad. The AI does not know whether you want a definition, business ideas, advice about starting a business, an explanation of profit, a marketing plan, or something else. The AI can still respond, but it has to make assumptions about what you want.

lesson_blocks.title: Better Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Explain how a small business earns money.

lesson_blocks.title: Why This Is Better
lesson_blocks.content: This prompt gives the AI a clear task: explain how a small business earns money. The subject is narrower and the expected response is easier to understand. However, the AI still does not know the learner’s level or which business example would be most useful.

lesson_blocks.title: Stronger Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Explain how a small retail business earns money to a complete beginner. Explain revenue, expenses, and profit using a simple clothing-store example.

lesson_blocks.title: Why This Prompt Is Stronger
lesson_blocks.content: This version provides several useful instructions. It identifies the topic, specifies that the explanation is for a complete beginner, identifies the concepts that should be covered, and asks for a clothing-store example. The AI therefore has much more information about the response you want.

lesson_blocks.title: A Useful Principle
lesson_blocks.content: A longer prompt is not automatically a better prompt. The goal is clarity, not unnecessary length. Include the information that helps the AI understand the task and the result you need.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice
lesson_blocks.content: Choose a topic you know well. First write a one-word or very broad prompt about it. Then rewrite the prompt so that it clearly explains what you want the AI to do, who the response is for, and what information should be included. Compare the two prompts.

episodes.title: The Foundation Prompt Formula
episodes.description: Learn a simple four-part framework for writing clearer AI prompts using Task, Context, Details, and Format.

lesson_blocks.title: The Foundation Prompt Formula
lesson_blocks.content: Following a clear structure when giving instructions to AI can improve your chances of receiving a useful response. There are many ways to design prompts, but a practical foundation for beginners is: TASK + CONTEXT + DETAILS + FORMAT. You do not have to use every part in every prompt. The framework helps you think about what information the AI needs in order to understand your request clearly.

lesson_blocks.title: 1. Task — What Should AI Do?
lesson_blocks.content: The task tells the AI the main action you want it to perform. A useful prompt should make this action clear. Common task words include explain, write, summarize, compare, create, analyze, list, rewrite, and suggest.

lesson_blocks.title: Task Example
lesson_blocks.content: Write an email.

lesson_blocks.title: 2. Context — Why Do You Need It?
lesson_blocks.content: Context gives the AI background information about the situation. It helps explain why the task is being performed and can make the response more relevant to your circumstances.

lesson_blocks.title: Context Example
lesson_blocks.content: I missed yesterday's class.

lesson_blocks.title: 3. Details — What Should Be Included?
lesson_blocks.content: Details specify the important information, requirements, or points that should appear in the response. Without useful details, the AI may leave out something that matters to you or make assumptions about what should be included.

lesson_blocks.title: Details Example
lesson_blocks.content: Apologize and ask what assignment I missed.

lesson_blocks.title: 4. Format — How Should the Answer Look?
lesson_blocks.content: Format tells the AI how you want the response presented. You might request an email, table, numbered steps, bullet points, paragraph, checklist, specific word limit, or another suitable structure. You can also specify an appropriate tone when that matters.

lesson_blocks.title: Format Example
lesson_blocks.content: Professional and under 100 words.

lesson_blocks.title: Putting the Four Parts Together
lesson_blocks.content: The four pieces can now be combined into one clear instruction. Notice that the final prompt tells the AI what to do, provides the situation, identifies what must be included, and describes how the response should be written.

lesson_blocks.title: Complete Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Write a professional email to my instructor explaining that I missed yesterday's class. Apologize and ask which assignment I need to complete. Keep it polite and under 100 words.

lesson_blocks.title: How to Think Before You Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Before sending an important prompt, ask yourself four questions: What do I want the AI to do? What background does it need? What important details should it include? How should the final answer be presented? If some of these questions are not relevant to the task, you do not need to force them into the prompt. The purpose of the formula is to improve clarity.

lesson_blocks.title: Exercise — Improve the Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Improve this prompt: "Tell me about jobs." Use the Foundation Prompt Formula where appropriate. Decide on the task, provide useful context, add relevant details, and specify the format you would like the answer to use.

episodes.title: Iteration
episodes.description: Learn how to improve AI responses through follow-up instructions instead of expecting the perfect result from the first prompt.

lesson_blocks.title: What Is Iteration?
lesson_blocks.content: Iteration means improving AI results through additional instructions. Instead of expecting the perfect response from your first prompt, you can review what the AI produced and then provide another instruction explaining what you want changed, clarified, expanded, shortened, or presented differently.

lesson_blocks.title: Prompting Can Be a Conversation
lesson_blocks.content: When using a conversational Generative AI system, you can often continue working in the same chat. The AI can use the earlier conversation as context, allowing you to refine the response step by step. This means you do not always need to rewrite your entire original prompt when only one part of the response needs improvement.

lesson_blocks.title: The Iteration Process
lesson_blocks.content:
A simple iteration process is:

1. PROMPT — Give the AI your initial instruction.

2. REVIEW — Read the response carefully.

3. IDENTIFY — Decide what is missing, unclear, incorrect, too long, too technical, or otherwise unsuitable for your purpose.

4. REFINE — Give the AI a specific follow-up instruction.

5. REVIEW AGAIN — Check whether the new response is better and whether important information needs verification.

You can repeat this process until the result is suitable for your purpose.

lesson_blocks.title: Examples of Follow-Up Instructions
lesson_blocks.content: After receiving an AI response, you might ask it to make the answer simpler, make it shorter, give another example, make it more professional, turn the information into a table, explain a particular step again, provide five alternatives, or make the explanation suitable for high-school students. Each follow-up instruction tells the AI how you want the existing response improved.

lesson_blocks.title: Make It Simpler
lesson_blocks.content: Make it simpler.

lesson_blocks.title: Make It Shorter
lesson_blocks.content: Make it shorter.

lesson_blocks.title: Ask for Another Example
lesson_blocks.content: Give me another example.

lesson_blocks.title: Change the Tone
lesson_blocks.content: Make it more professional.

lesson_blocks.title: Change the Format
lesson_blocks.content: Turn this into a table.

lesson_blocks.title: Ask for Clarification
lesson_blocks.content: Explain step 2 again using simpler language and an example.

lesson_blocks.title: Ask for Alternatives
lesson_blocks.content: Give me five alternatives.

lesson_blocks.title: Adapt for an Audience
lesson_blocks.content: Make it suitable for high-school students.

lesson_blocks.title: Be Specific About What Needs Improvement
lesson_blocks.content: Useful iteration is more than repeatedly asking the AI to "make it better." Try to identify what should change. For example, you can say that the explanation is too technical, the email is too long, an example is unclear, or a particular section needs more detail. Specific feedback gives the AI clearer direction for the next response.

lesson_blocks.title: Iteration Does Not Guarantee Accuracy
lesson_blocks.content: A response can become clearer and better written through iteration and still contain incorrect information. Continue applying the foundation rule from Unit 1: ASK → REVIEW → VERIFY → USE. Important facts, claims, calculations, and decisions should be checked when appropriate.

lesson_blocks.title: Check Your Understanding
lesson_blocks.content: What is iteration? Explain it in your own words and give two examples of follow-up instructions you could use to improve an AI response.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice Iteration
lesson_blocks.content: Give a Generative AI system a simple prompt on a topic you understand. Review its response and identify one thing you would improve. Give the AI a specific follow-up instruction. Repeat the process at least twice and compare the original response with the final response.

episodes.title: Unit 2 Worksheet — Prompt Improvement Practice
episodes.description: Practice improving weak or overly broad prompts by adding a clear task, useful context, relevant details, and an appropriate output format.

lesson_blocks.title: Prompt Improvement Practice
lesson_blocks.content: This worksheet gives you three broad or unclear prompts to improve. Apply what you learned in this unit about clear tasks, context, details, format, and audience. There may be more than one good way to improve each prompt. The goal is to make your instruction specific enough for the AI to understand the result you want.

lesson_blocks.title: Before You Begin
lesson_blocks.content:
For each prompt, consider:

TASK — What exactly should the AI do?

CONTEXT — What background information would help?

DETAILS — What should the response include?

FORMAT — How should the response be presented?

You do not have to include every element if it is not relevant. Use the information that makes your request clearer.

lesson_blocks.title: Exercise 1 — Improve the Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Improve this prompt: "Write something." Rewrite it so the AI knows what to write, who the content is intended for, what it should communicate, and any useful length or format requirements.

lesson_blocks.title: Exercise 2 — Improve the Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Improve this prompt: "Marketing." Rewrite it as a clear instruction for an AI system. Decide what is being marketed, what you want the AI to produce, the intended audience or business context where appropriate, and the format of the response.

lesson_blocks.title: Exercise 3 — Improve the Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Improve this prompt: "Interview." Rewrite it so the AI clearly understands the type of interview, the role or situation, what you want it to generate, and any useful details about the response.

lesson_blocks.title: Review Your Prompts
lesson_blocks.content: Before comparing your work with the model answers, review each prompt you created. Ask yourself whether another person could read the prompt and clearly understand what result you want. If the instruction is still too broad, refine it before continuing.

Your wording does not need to be identical. A good answer should communicate the task clearly and provide enough relevant information for the AI to understand the result you want.

lesson_blocks.title: Assignment Model Answers
lesson_blocks.content: Review the five model prompts below after completing the Unit 2 assignment. Notice how each prompt gives the AI a specific task and adds useful requirements for the expected response.

lesson_blocks.title: 1. Education Prompt — Model Answer

lesson_blocks.title: 2. Email Prompt — Model Answer

lesson_blocks.title: 3. Business Prompt — Model Answer

lesson_blocks.title: 4. Career Prompt — Model Answer

lesson_blocks.title: 5. Research Prompt — Model Answer

lesson_blocks.title: Worksheet Model Answers
lesson_blocks.content: Now compare your three rewritten worksheet prompts with the model answers below. Focus on what information was added to transform each broad prompt into a useful instruction.

title: Applying AI
description: Learn how to apply Artificial Intelligence practically in education, workplace tasks, career development, and business activities.

episodes.title: AI for Education
episodes.description: Learn practical ways Artificial Intelligence can support learning, studying, practice, revision, and understanding difficult concepts.

lesson_blocks.title: Using AI for Education
lesson_blocks.content: Artificial Intelligence can support learning in many practical ways. It can help you understand a topic, practise what you have learned, organize your studies, and receive explanations presented in different ways. AI should be used as a learning assistant rather than as a replacement for studying, thinking, or verifying important information.

lesson_blocks.title: Ways AI Can Support Learning
lesson_blocks.content:
AI can help learners:

- Understand difficult topics
- Generate examples
- Create study schedules
- Create quizzes
- Review answers
- Generate flashcards
- Practice languages
- Summarize information

These uses can be combined. For example, you might first ask AI to explain a topic, then request examples, and finally ask it to test your understanding.

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding Difficult Topics
lesson_blocks.content: When a topic feels difficult, you can ask AI to explain it at your current level. Instead of simply asking for an answer, ask for an explanation that helps you understand the reasoning or concept. You can also request simpler language, examples, analogies, or a step-by-step explanation.

lesson_blocks.title: Example — Learning a Difficult Topic
lesson_blocks.content: Teach me photosynthesis as a complete beginner. Explain it in five simple steps.

lesson_blocks.title: Improve Understanding Through Follow-Up Prompts
lesson_blocks.content: Your first AI response does not have to be the end of the learning process. You can use iteration, which you learned in the previous unit, to ask the AI to explain the same concept differently or test whether you understood it.

lesson_blocks.title: Follow-Up Prompt 1
lesson_blocks.content: Give me an everyday analogy.

lesson_blocks.title: Follow-Up Prompt 2
lesson_blocks.content: Test me with five questions.

lesson_blocks.title: AI as a Study and Practice Assistant
lesson_blocks.content: AI can also help organize learning. A learner may ask for a study schedule based on available time, generate flashcards for revision, create practice questions, practise a language conversation, or summarize material into key points. The quality of the result depends partly on how clearly you explain your learning goal and provide relevant context.

lesson_blocks.title: Use AI to Learn, Not Just to Produce Answers
lesson_blocks.content: If AI completes every exercise for you, you may receive an answer without developing the skill yourself. Use AI to explain, demonstrate, question, give feedback, and support your practice. Review its responses critically and verify important information when necessary.

lesson_blocks.title: Check Your Understanding
lesson_blocks.content: Give five ways AI can support learning. Try to answer from memory before reviewing the lesson.

lesson_blocks.title: Model Answer
lesson_blocks.content:
Five examples are:

1. Explain difficult concepts.
2. Generate practice questions.
3. Create study plans.
4. Summarize information.
5. Provide feedback.

Other appropriate examples from this lesson may also be valid, such as generating flashcards or supporting language practice.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Use AI as a Learning Assistant
lesson_blocks.content: Choose a topic you are currently learning or would like to understand. Write a prompt asking AI to teach the topic at your level. After receiving the response, use at least two follow-up prompts to improve your understanding. For example, request an analogy, another example, a simpler explanation, or a short quiz.

episodes.title: AI for Work
episodes.description: Learn practical ways Artificial Intelligence can support everyday workplace tasks such as emails, reports, summaries, presentations, planning, brainstorming, and organizing information.

lesson_blocks.title: Using AI at Work
lesson_blocks.content: Artificial Intelligence can assist with many everyday workplace tasks, especially tasks involving writing, organizing information, summarizing content, generating ideas, and preparing drafts. The goal is not simply to make AI do the work for you. It is to use AI as a tool that can help you work more efficiently while you remain responsible for reviewing and approving the final result.

lesson_blocks.title: Workplace Tasks AI Can Support
lesson_blocks.content:
AI may assist with:

- Emails
- Reports
- Meeting summaries
- Presentations
- Planning
- Brainstorming
- Document organization

These are examples of assistance. The exact way AI should be used depends on the task, the organization, the information involved, and the organization's policies.

lesson_blocks.title: Writing and Communication
lesson_blocks.content: AI can help prepare first drafts of emails, reports, presentation content, and other workplace communication. A useful prompt should explain what needs to be written, who it is for, the important information to include, and the tone or format required. The person using AI should still review the result before sending or publishing it.

lesson_blocks.title: Summarizing and Organizing Information
lesson_blocks.content: Workplace information is not always received in a clean or organized format. You may have meeting notes, observations, updates, or several points written quickly. AI can help group related information, identify important points, and present the material in a clearer structure.

lesson_blocks.title: Planning and Brainstorming
lesson_blocks.content: AI can also support planning and brainstorming. For example, you might ask it to suggest possible agenda items for a meeting, organize tasks into a simple plan, generate ideas for a presentation, or propose different approaches to a workplace problem. These suggestions should be treated as ideas to evaluate rather than decisions that must automatically be followed.

lesson_blocks.title: Exercise — Organize Raw Workplace Notes
lesson_blocks.content:
Imagine you receive the following raw notes:

Sales improved 10%. Delivery complaints increased. Staff need training. New campaign starts Monday.

How would you organize these notes so that a manager can quickly understand the important information? Try creating your own structured version before reviewing the model answer below.

lesson_blocks.title: Model Answer
lesson_blocks.content:
Performance: Sales increased by 10%.

Challenges: Delivery-related complaints increased.

Staff Needs: Additional training may be required.

Next Steps: Launch the new campaign on Monday and monitor its impact alongside delivery performance.

lesson_blocks.title: What Changed?
lesson_blocks.content: The model answer does not simply repeat the raw notes. It organizes the information into meaningful categories: performance, challenges, staff needs, and next steps. This makes the same information easier to scan and use. AI can assist with this kind of transformation when you clearly describe the result you need.

lesson_blocks.title: Review Workplace AI Outputs
lesson_blocks.content: AI-generated workplace content should be reviewed before it is used. Check names, dates, figures, claims, instructions, and other important details. Also consider whether the information is confidential or sensitive before providing it to an AI system. Follow your organization’s approved AI, privacy, confidentiality, and security policies.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Turn Notes Into a Workplace Update
lesson_blocks.content: Write four or five short notes about an imaginary workplace situation. Then create a prompt asking AI to organize the notes into a clear professional update. Specify the audience and the format you want. Review the result and identify anything that needs to be corrected or improved before it could be used at work.

episodes.title: AI for Career Development
episodes.description: Learn how Artificial Intelligence can support career development through CV and cover-letter preparation, interview practice, skills planning, job understanding, and career research.

lesson_blocks.title: Using AI for Career Development
lesson_blocks.content: Artificial Intelligence can support you at different stages of career development. It can help you understand career options, improve how you present your skills, prepare for job applications, practise interviews, and plan the skills you may need to develop. AI should support your career decisions rather than make those decisions for you.

lesson_blocks.title: Ways AI Can Support Your Career
lesson_blocks.content:
AI can assist with:

- CV wording
- Cover letters
- Interview practice
- Skills planning
- Explaining job descriptions
- Career research

These activities can be useful whether you are looking for your first job, changing careers, preparing for a promotion, or developing new professional skills.

lesson_blocks.title: CV Wording
lesson_blocks.content: AI can help improve the wording and clarity of a CV. For example, you can provide information about work you have genuinely performed and ask AI to help express it professionally. Always review the result carefully. Your CV should accurately represent your real education, skills, responsibilities, and achievements.

lesson_blocks.title: Cover Letters
lesson_blocks.content: A cover letter should connect your genuine experience and abilities to a particular opportunity. AI can help organize a draft when you provide the role, relevant information about yourself, and the points you want emphasized. Avoid using AI to invent qualifications or experience that you do not have.

lesson_blocks.title: Interview Practice
lesson_blocks.content: AI can act as a practice interviewer. You can tell it which role you are preparing for and ask it to present questions one at a time. You can then answer each question and request feedback. This allows you to practise explaining your experience before attending a real interview.

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding Job Descriptions
lesson_blocks.content: Job descriptions may contain unfamiliar responsibilities, requirements, or terminology. AI can help explain these in simpler language. You can also ask it to identify the main skills mentioned in a job description so that you can understand what the employer is seeking. You should still refer to the original job description when deciding whether you meet the requirements.

lesson_blocks.title: Career Research and Skills Planning
lesson_blocks.content: AI can help you explore a career and organize a learning plan. For example, you can ask what skills are commonly associated with a particular career, what a beginner should learn first, and how those skills could be developed over several months. Treat the response as a starting point for further research because career requirements can differ between employers, industries, and locations.

lesson_blocks.title: Example — Career Roadmap Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: I want to become a digital marketer. Create a six-month beginner learning roadmap showing the most important skills to learn.

lesson_blocks.title: Making the Career Roadmap More Useful
lesson_blocks.content: The example gives AI a clear task, but it can be improved further by adding your circumstances. You might tell AI how many hours you can study each week, what you already know, the type of digital marketing work that interests you, and whether you want practical projects included. This makes the roadmap more relevant to your situation.

lesson_blocks.title: Keep Career Information Accurate
lesson_blocks.content: AI can help you communicate your real abilities more clearly, but it should not be used to fabricate education, employment history, qualifications, achievements, or skills. Review career documents carefully and verify important career information before acting on it.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Build a Career Development Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Choose a career or job role that interests you. Ask AI to explain the role to a complete beginner and identify important skills associated with it. Then ask for a learning roadmap based on your current level and available study time. Review the response and identify which recommendations you would need to verify before relying on them.

episodes.title: AI for Business
episodes.description: Learn practical ways Artificial Intelligence can support business activities, decision-making, customer understanding, communication, planning, and problem-solving.

lesson_blocks.title: Using AI for Business
lesson_blocks.content: Artificial Intelligence can support many everyday business activities involving ideas, communication, planning, research, and organizing information. A business can use AI to assist people with these tasks, but the business and its staff remain responsible for reviewing outputs and making decisions.

lesson_blocks.title: Ways AI Can Support a Business
lesson_blocks.content:
AI may assist with:

- Marketing ideas
- Product descriptions
- Customer-response drafts
- FAQs
- Sales scripts
- Content planning
- Customer feedback summaries
- Research support

These are examples of business uses. Whether AI is appropriate depends on the task, the information involved, and the level of human review required.

lesson_blocks.title: Marketing Ideas and Content Planning
lesson_blocks.content: AI can help a business generate and organize marketing ideas. For example, a business can describe its products, customers, goals, communication channels, and available resources, then ask AI to suggest possible content or campaign ideas. The business should evaluate the suggestions before using them.

lesson_blocks.title: Product Descriptions and Sales Scripts
lesson_blocks.content: AI can help draft product descriptions and sales scripts when it is given accurate information about the product or service. The final content should be reviewed to make sure it does not contain invented features, incorrect prices, unsupported claims, or promises the business cannot fulfil.

lesson_blocks.title: Customer Responses and FAQs
lesson_blocks.content: Businesses often answer similar customer questions repeatedly. AI can help draft responses and organize frequently asked questions using approved business information. Human review is especially important when a request involves complaints, payments, refunds, unusual circumstances, or information the AI has not been authorized to provide.

lesson_blocks.title: Customer Feedback Summaries
lesson_blocks.content: When a business receives many customer comments, AI may help summarize recurring themes and organize feedback into useful categories. This can make large amounts of written feedback easier to review. Important conclusions should still be checked against the original information before decisions are made.

lesson_blocks.title: Research Support
lesson_blocks.content: AI can support early-stage business research by helping generate questions, explain unfamiliar topics, organize information, or identify areas that may require further investigation. AI-generated research should not automatically be treated as verified evidence. Important facts, statistics, prices, regulations, competitors, and market claims should be checked using reliable sources.

lesson_blocks.title: Business Exercise — Bakery Content Plan
lesson_blocks.content: Create a seven-day content plan for a bakery. Think about how the bakery could vary its content across the week instead of publishing the same type of message every day. Complete your own plan before reviewing the model answer.

lesson_blocks.title: Model Answer
lesson_blocks.content:
Day 1: Product spotlight
Day 2: Behind-the-scenes baking
Day 3: Customer question
Day 4: Educational baking tip
Day 5: Weekend promotion
Day 6: Customer testimonial
Day 7: Thank-you and order reminder

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Model Answer
lesson_blocks.content: The model answer creates variety across the seven days. Some content promotes products, some shows how the business works, some encourages customer interaction, and some provides useful information. This demonstrates how AI can help organize an initial content plan that a business can then review and adapt.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Apply AI to a Business
lesson_blocks.content: Choose a small business such as a restaurant, salon, shop, hotel, repair business, or another business you understand. Select one business task from this lesson and write a clear prompt asking AI to assist with it. Review the response and identify what information would need to be checked before the business could use it.

lesson_blocks.title: Business Decisions Still Require Human Judgment
lesson_blocks.content: AI-generated business content may contain mistakes, unsuitable recommendations, or invented information. Review outputs before communicating with customers or making business decisions. Do not provide confidential, personal, or sensitive business information to an AI system unless its use is authorized and appropriate.

lesson_blocks.title: Review Your Assignment
lesson_blocks.content: Complete the Unit 3 practical assignment before reviewing this model answer. Your improved prompt does not have to use exactly the same wording. Compare how much useful context and how many practical constraints your prompt provides compared with the original weak prompt.

lesson_blocks.title: First Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Make a timetable.

lesson_blocks.title: Why the First Prompt Is Weak
lesson_blocks.content: The prompt does not provide enough information. It does not tell the AI who the timetable is for, which subjects need to be studied, how much time is available, or how the week should be organized.

lesson_blocks.title: Improved Prompt — Model Answer
lesson_blocks.content: Create a Monday-to-Sunday study timetable for a university student studying mathematics, English, economics, and computer studies. I have two hours each weekday evening and four hours on Saturday. Sunday should focus on revision.

lesson_blocks.title: Why the Improved Prompt Is More Useful
lesson_blocks.content: The improved prompt gives the AI specific context and constraints. It identifies the learner, the subjects, the days to cover, the available study time, and the purpose of Sunday. This gives the AI enough information to produce a timetable that is much more relevant to the learner’s situation.

lesson_blocks.title: Lesson Learned
lesson_blocks.content: Providing specific context and constraints produces a more useful result.

lesson_blocks.title: Reflect on Your Prompt
lesson_blocks.content: Compare your improved prompt with the model answer. Identify the context and constraints you included. If any important information is missing, revise your prompt and test it again. Compare the new AI response with the response from your previous prompt.

title: AI Accuracy, Privacy, and Responsibility
description: Learn how to recognize AI errors, verify AI-generated information, protect privacy, and use Artificial Intelligence responsibly.

episodes.title: AI Errors
episodes.description: Learn how Artificial Intelligence can produce incorrect, invented, misleading, unsupported, or outdated information and why AI-generated claims must be reviewed critically.

lesson_blocks.title: AI Can Produce Errors
lesson_blocks.content: Artificial Intelligence can generate useful and convincing responses, but those responses are not automatically correct. An AI system may produce information that sounds clear, detailed, and confident while still containing errors. This is why AI-generated information should be reviewed rather than accepted automatically.

lesson_blocks.title: Types of AI Errors
lesson_blocks.content:
AI may produce:

- Incorrect facts
- Wrong dates
- Invented information
- Misleading explanations
- Unsupported statistics
- Outdated information

Some errors may be easy to notice, while others can appear believable and require verification.

lesson_blocks.title: Incorrect Facts and Wrong Dates
lesson_blocks.content: AI may give a fact or date that is incorrect. For example, it may associate an event with the wrong year or provide inaccurate information about a person, organization, product, or subject. A well-written answer does not prove that these details are correct.

lesson_blocks.title: Invented Information
lesson_blocks.content: Sometimes AI may generate information that appears to be factual even though the information is not supported. It may invent details, references, events, names, or explanations. This can be especially difficult for a learner to detect when the response is written confidently.

lesson_blocks.title: Misleading Explanations
lesson_blocks.content: An AI response may contain some correct information but still create a misleading overall impression. Important context may be missing, a complicated issue may be oversimplified, or different ideas may be combined incorrectly. Reviewing the reasoning and context is therefore important, not just checking individual words.

lesson_blocks.title: Unsupported Statistics
lesson_blocks.content: Numbers and percentages can make a response appear authoritative. However, an AI system may provide a statistic without a reliable supporting source. Before relying on an important statistic, check where it came from, when the underlying information was published, and whether the source actually supports the claim.

lesson_blocks.title: Outdated Information
lesson_blocks.content: Some information changes over time. Prices, laws, policies, software, job requirements, business information, schedules, and many other facts may become outdated. When current information matters, check an appropriate up-to-date source instead of assuming an AI response reflects the latest situation.

lesson_blocks.title: What Is an AI Hallucination?
lesson_blocks.content: When an AI produces information that is incorrect or invented but presents it as though it were valid, this is sometimes called an AI hallucination. The important lesson is that a confident or professional-sounding response should not automatically be treated as evidence that a claim is true.

lesson_blocks.title: Exercise — Question the Claim
lesson_blocks.content: AI states: “87% of employers now require AI skills.” What should you ask before accepting or using this claim? Think about how you would determine whether the statistic is trustworthy.

lesson_blocks.title: Model Answer
lesson_blocks.content:
Ask:

- What is the source?
- Who conducted the study?
- When was it published?
- Is the source reliable?
- Does the source actually support this claim?

lesson_blocks.title: Why These Questions Matter
lesson_blocks.content: These questions move you from simply accepting a claim to examining its evidence. A statistic is more useful when you can identify its original source, understand who produced it and when, evaluate the reliability of that source, and confirm that the source actually says what the AI claims it says.

lesson_blocks.title: Confidence Is Not Proof
lesson_blocks.content: Do not use the confidence, length, formatting, or professional tone of an AI response as proof of accuracy. Important claims should be checked against appropriate reliable sources before they are used for decisions, assignments, professional work, or public communication.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Identify What Needs Verification
lesson_blocks.content: Ask an AI system a question about a topic you know something about. Review its answer and identify at least three claims that could be checked. For each claim, decide what type of source or evidence you would need in order to verify it.

episodes.title: Verifying AI Information
episodes.description: Learn a simple four-step process for reviewing and verifying AI-generated information before using it.

lesson_blocks.title: A Simple Process for Using AI Information
lesson_blocks.content:
AI can help you find explanations, generate ideas, summarize information, and answer questions. However, receiving an answer from AI is only the beginning. Before relying on important AI-generated information, use this four-step process:

ASK → REVIEW → VERIFY → USE

lesson_blocks.title: Step 1 — ASK
lesson_blocks.content: ASK: Ask the question. Start by clearly telling the AI what information or assistance you need. A clear question gives the AI a better opportunity to provide a relevant response, but you should not assume that the response will automatically be correct.

lesson_blocks.title: Step 2 — REVIEW
lesson_blocks.content: REVIEW: Read critically. Examine the AI response carefully instead of accepting it immediately. Ask yourself whether the answer makes sense, whether anything appears unclear or inconsistent, and which claims may need further checking.

lesson_blocks.title: Step 3 — VERIFY
lesson_blocks.content: VERIFY: Check reliable sources when necessary. Important facts, dates, statistics, quotations, references, rules, or other claims may need to be confirmed using appropriate reliable sources. Verification is especially important when an error could affect an assignment, professional task, business decision, or another important outcome.

lesson_blocks.title: Step 4 — USE
lesson_blocks.content: USE: Use the information only after determining that it is suitable for your purpose. After reviewing and, where necessary, verifying the information, decide whether it is accurate, relevant, appropriate, and useful for what you are trying to accomplish.

lesson_blocks.title: Putting the Four Steps Together
lesson_blocks.content:
The process is:

1. ASK — Ask the question.
2. REVIEW — Read the response critically.
3. VERIFY — Check reliable sources when necessary.
4. USE — Use the information only after determining that it is suitable for your purpose.

The important habit is not to move directly from asking AI a question to using its answer without first reviewing it.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — ASK, REVIEW, VERIFY, USE
lesson_blocks.content: Choose a topic and ask an AI system a factual question. Read the response critically and identify one claim that could be checked. Find an appropriate reliable source for that claim. Compare the source with the AI response, then decide whether the AI-generated information is suitable for your purpose.

lesson_blocks.title: Develop a Verification Habit
lesson_blocks.content: You do not need to treat every AI response in exactly the same way. The amount of verification required depends on what you are using the information for. A brainstorming suggestion may require little checking, while an important factual claim may require careful verification. The goal is to develop the habit of thinking critically before using AI-generated information.

episodes.title: Privacy and Security
episodes.description: Learn how to protect sensitive information when using AI tools and how to make safer decisions about organizational and customer data.

lesson_blocks.title: Privacy and Security When Using AI
lesson_blocks.content: AI tools can be useful for working with information, documents, and business tasks. However, you must think carefully about the information you provide to an AI system. Information that is private, confidential, sensitive, or protected should not be shared unnecessarily.

lesson_blocks.title: Information You Should Protect
lesson_blocks.content:
Avoid unnecessarily sharing:

- Passwords
- PIN numbers
- Banking credentials
- Confidential customer data
- Sensitive business information
- Private health information
- Government identification numbers

lesson_blocks.title: Passwords and PIN Numbers
lesson_blocks.content: Passwords and PIN numbers are authentication information used to protect access to accounts, systems, devices, and services. They should not be placed into an AI prompt simply because the AI is helping you solve a related problem.

lesson_blocks.title: Banking Credentials
lesson_blocks.content: Banking credentials can provide access to financial accounts or transactions. When asking AI for help with a financial or payment-related task, avoid including credentials or other sensitive authentication information that is not necessary for the question.

lesson_blocks.title: Customer and Business Information
lesson_blocks.content: Confidential customer data and sensitive business information may belong to an organization or another person rather than to you personally. Having access to information does not automatically mean you have permission to upload it to an AI system.

lesson_blocks.title: Health and Identification Information
lesson_blocks.content: Private health information and government identification numbers can be highly sensitive personal information. Consider whether the information is actually necessary for the AI task and whether you are authorized to share it before entering it into an AI system.

lesson_blocks.title: Follow Organizational Policies
lesson_blocks.content: Always follow the organization’s privacy and security policies. An organization may also have confidentiality requirements and rules about which AI tools are approved for workplace use.

lesson_blocks.title: Scenario — Customer Database
lesson_blocks.content: A manager asks an employee to upload the company’s customer database into an AI tool. What should the employee do? Think about privacy, security, confidentiality, authorization, and whether the AI tool is approved for this use.

lesson_blocks.title: Scenario Answer
lesson_blocks.content: The employee should first check company privacy, security, confidentiality, and approved AI-use policies. Sensitive customer data should not be uploaded without appropriate authorization and safeguards.

lesson_blocks.title: Why Authorization Matters
lesson_blocks.content: A request from another person does not remove the need to follow privacy and security requirements. Before sensitive organizational or customer information is provided to an AI system, the employee should determine whether the organization permits that use and whether the required safeguards are in place.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Decide Before You Share
lesson_blocks.content: Imagine you are using an AI tool at work. Before entering information into it, ask: Is this information sensitive? Do I need to include it? Am I authorized to share it? Is this AI tool approved for this type of information? What organizational policies apply?

episodes.title: Responsible AI
episodes.description: Learn the core principles of responsible AI use, including accuracy, privacy, security, fairness, human oversight, transparency, permissions, and respect for intellectual property.

lesson_blocks.title: What Is Responsible AI Use?
lesson_blocks.content:
Responsible AI use means using Artificial Intelligence in a way that considers the quality of the information, the people affected, the information being handled, and the consequences of using the AI output.

Responsible AI use includes:

- Accuracy
- Privacy
- Security
- Fairness
- Human oversight
- Transparency
- Appropriate permissions
- Respect for intellectual property

lesson_blocks.title: Accuracy
lesson_blocks.content: Accuracy means paying attention to whether AI-generated information is correct and suitable for its intended purpose. Important facts and claims should be reviewed and, when necessary, verified before they are relied upon.

lesson_blocks.title: Privacy
lesson_blocks.content: Privacy means protecting personal, confidential, and sensitive information. Before providing information to an AI system, consider whether the information needs to be shared and whether you are permitted to share it.

lesson_blocks.title: Security
lesson_blocks.content: Security means protecting information, accounts, systems, and organizational resources from inappropriate access or exposure. AI should be used in ways that follow applicable security requirements and safeguards.

lesson_blocks.title: Fairness
lesson_blocks.content: Fairness means considering whether the use or output of an AI system could treat people or groups unfairly. AI-generated recommendations and decisions should be reviewed carefully when they may affect people.

lesson_blocks.title: Human Oversight
lesson_blocks.content: Human oversight means people remain involved in reviewing AI outputs and making appropriate decisions. AI can assist with a task, but a person may still need to check the result, apply judgment, correct mistakes, or decide whether the output should be used.

lesson_blocks.title: Transparency
lesson_blocks.content: Transparency means being appropriately clear about the role AI has played. In situations where it matters, people should understand that AI was used to generate, assist with, analyze, or prepare information.

lesson_blocks.title: Appropriate Permissions
lesson_blocks.content: Appropriate permissions means making sure you are authorized to use the information, systems, tools, or resources involved in an AI task. Access to information does not automatically mean permission to provide that information to an AI system.

lesson_blocks.title: Respect for Intellectual Property
lesson_blocks.content: Respect for intellectual property means considering ownership and permitted use of material such as written content, images, software, designs, research, and other protected work when using AI. AI use does not remove the need to respect applicable ownership and usage rights.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Apply the Principles
lesson_blocks.content: Think of one way you currently use or could use AI for education, work, or business. Review that use against the eight principles: accuracy, privacy, security, fairness, human oversight, transparency, appropriate permissions, and respect for intellectual property. Identify any principle that requires additional attention before you use the AI output.

lesson_blocks.title: Responsible AI Requires Judgment
lesson_blocks.content: Responsible AI is not only about whether an AI system can perform a task. It also requires considering whether the task and the resulting information are being handled appropriately. The person using AI remains responsible for applying suitable judgment, policies, permissions, and safeguards.

lesson_blocks.title: Model Answer — Scenario 1
lesson_blocks.content: Do not rely on it automatically. Verify with qualified healthcare professionals and reliable medical sources.

lesson_blocks.title: Why This Response Is Appropriate
lesson_blocks.content: Serious medical information can affect a person’s health and safety. An AI response should not automatically be treated as professional medical advice. The information should be checked using appropriate reliable medical sources and qualified healthcare professionals.

lesson_blocks.title: Scenario 2 — AI-Drafted Advertisement
lesson_blocks.content: AI drafts an advertisement.

lesson_blocks.title: Model Answer — Scenario 2
lesson_blocks.content: Review the advertisement before publishing for accuracy, misleading claims, brand suitability, and other relevant concerns.

lesson_blocks.title: Why This Response Is Appropriate
lesson_blocks.content: AI can help prepare advertising content, but the organization remains responsible for what it publishes. Human review can identify inaccurate statements, misleading claims, unsuitable wording, brand issues, or other concerns before the advertisement reaches the public.

lesson_blocks.title: Scenario 3 — Statistic Without a Source
lesson_blocks.content: AI produces a statistic without a source.

lesson_blocks.title: Model Answer — Scenario 3
lesson_blocks.content: Do not use the statistic until it has been independently verified.

lesson_blocks.title: Why This Response Is Appropriate
lesson_blocks.content: A statistic can appear convincing simply because it contains a precise number or percentage. Without supporting evidence, you do not know whether the figure is accurate, current, or correctly represented. Independent verification should happen before the statistic is relied upon.

lesson_blocks.content: Compare your three responses with the model answers. For each scenario, identify the principle you applied, such as accuracy, verification, human oversight, or responsible AI use. Revise any answer where you now think an important consideration was missing.

title: Automating Tasks
description: Learn the foundations of automation, understand how workflows are structured, and explore when Artificial Intelligence should and should not be added to an automated process.

episodes.title: What Is Automation?
episodes.description: Learn what automation means and compare a manual process with a process where technology performs defined tasks automatically or with reduced manual work.

lesson_blocks.title: What Is Automation?
lesson_blocks.content: Automation means using technology to perform defined tasks automatically or with reduced manual work.

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding Automation
lesson_blocks.content: Many activities involve repeating the same steps whenever something happens. Automation allows technology to perform some or all of those defined steps instead of requiring a person to carry out every step manually each time.

lesson_blocks.title: Manual Process
lesson_blocks.content: Customer completes form → Employee reads form → Employee copies information → Employee sends confirmation → Employee updates records

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Manual Process
lesson_blocks.content: In this example, a person is involved throughout the process. After the customer completes the form, an employee must read it, copy the information, send a confirmation, and update the records. These are defined steps that may be repeated for every customer.

lesson_blocks.title: Automated Process
lesson_blocks.content: Form submitted → Information recorded → Confirmation sent → Team notified

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Automated Process
lesson_blocks.content: In the automated version, submitting the form can start a sequence of predefined actions. The information can be recorded, a confirmation can be sent, and the relevant team can be notified without requiring an employee to manually perform each step.

lesson_blocks.title: Manual and Automated Processes
lesson_blocks.content: The important difference is not that people disappear from the process. Automation reduces the amount of manual work required for defined tasks. People can still be involved where review, judgment, approval, communication, or exception handling is necessary.

lesson_blocks.title: Check Your Understanding
lesson_blocks.content: What is automation?

lesson_blocks.title: Answer
lesson_blocks.content: The use of technology to perform defined tasks automatically or with reduced human effort.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Identify an Automation Opportunity
lesson_blocks.content: Think of one repetitive task you perform in education, work, or business. Write down the steps in the current manual process. Then identify which defined steps could potentially be performed automatically by technology.

episodes.title: Workflows
episodes.description: Learn what a workflow is and understand how a process can be organized using a trigger, process, action, and result.

lesson_blocks.title: What Is a Workflow?
lesson_blocks.content: A workflow is a sequence of steps used to complete a process.

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding Workflows
lesson_blocks.content: A workflow shows how work moves from one step to another. Instead of thinking about a task as one large activity, we break it into smaller steps and identify what starts the process, what needs to happen, what action is performed, and what result should be produced.

lesson_blocks.title: The Basic Workflow Structure
lesson_blocks.content: TRIGGER → PROCESS → ACTION → RESULT

lesson_blocks.title: Trigger
lesson_blocks.content: The trigger is the event that starts the workflow. Something happens first, and that event causes the remaining steps to begin.

lesson_blocks.title: Process
lesson_blocks.content: The process is the work that needs to happen after the workflow has been triggered. This may involve checking, organizing, transforming, or evaluating information.

lesson_blocks.title: Action
lesson_blocks.content: The action is what the workflow does after processing the information. For example, it may save information, send a message, create a record, or notify someone.

lesson_blocks.title: Result
lesson_blocks.content: The result is the outcome produced after the workflow completes its defined steps. A useful workflow should have a clear result that helps accomplish the purpose of the process.

lesson_blocks.title: Example — Student Application Workflow
lesson_blocks.content:
Trigger: Student submits application.

Process: Check required fields.

Action: Record application and send acknowledgement.

Result: Student knows the application was received.

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Example
lesson_blocks.content: The student submitting the application starts the workflow. The required information is then checked. The application is recorded and an acknowledgement is sent. The final result is that the student receives confirmation that the application was received.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Design a Simple Workflow
lesson_blocks.content: Choose one simple process from education, work, or business. Describe it using the four-part structure: TRIGGER → PROCESS → ACTION → RESULT. Make sure you can clearly identify what starts the workflow and what result should be produced.

episodes.title: AI + Automation
episodes.description: Learn how AI can add capabilities such as language understanding, classification, generation, and prediction to automated processes, and understand when simple automation is sufficient without AI.

lesson_blocks.title: AI + Automation
lesson_blocks.content: AI may add language understanding, classification, generation, or prediction to an automated process.

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Difference
lesson_blocks.content: Automation and AI are related, but they are not the same thing. Automation follows defined steps to perform a process. AI can be added when part of that process requires capabilities such as understanding language, classifying information, generating content, or making predictions.

lesson_blocks.title: Language Understanding
lesson_blocks.content: AI can help a workflow interpret human language. For example, it can examine a customer message and determine what the customer is asking about.

lesson_blocks.title: Classification
lesson_blocks.content: AI can classify information into useful categories. A customer message, for example, might be classified as a payment issue, technical problem, sales inquiry, or another defined category.

lesson_blocks.title: Generation
lesson_blocks.content: AI can generate content as part of a workflow, such as preparing an initial response using appropriate information available to the process. The generated content may still require rules, safeguards, or human review depending on the situation.

lesson_blocks.title: Prediction
lesson_blocks.content: AI can also be used where a process requires a prediction based on available information. Whether prediction is appropriate depends on the purpose of the workflow and the information being used.

lesson_blocks.title: Example — Customer Payment Issue
lesson_blocks.content: The customer says: “I paid yesterday, but my account still says unpaid.”

lesson_blocks.title: Workflow
lesson_blocks.content: Message received → AI identifies category: payment issue → Approved payment-support information is retrieved → Initial response is generated → Account-specific issue is escalated to staff

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Workflow
lesson_blocks.content: The workflow begins when the message is received. AI helps identify the topic as a payment issue. Approved support information is then retrieved and an initial response is prepared. Because the customer has an account-specific problem, the issue is escalated to staff rather than leaving the entire process to AI.

lesson_blocks.title: Check Your Understanding
lesson_blocks.content: Does every automation need AI?

lesson_blocks.title: Answer
lesson_blocks.content: No.

lesson_blocks.title: Example — Automation Without AI
lesson_blocks.content: “Send a reminder every Monday at 9 AM.” For this, a simple automation is sufficient.

lesson_blocks.title: When Simple Automation Is Enough
lesson_blocks.content: If a task only needs to happen according to a clear rule, schedule, or predefined sequence, AI may not be necessary. Adding AI should serve a useful purpose rather than being added simply because AI is available.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — AI or Simple Automation?
lesson_blocks.content: Think of two repetitive tasks. For the first, choose a task that could be handled using a simple rule or schedule without AI. For the second, choose a task where language understanding, classification, generation, or prediction could make AI useful. Explain why you would or would not use AI in each case.

lesson_blocks.title: Scenario
lesson_blocks.content: A college receives 200 course inquiries every week.

lesson_blocks.title: Model Workflow
lesson_blocks.content: Inquiry received → Capture contact details → AI identifies topic → Approved course information retrieved → Response prepared → Inquiry logged → Complex request escalated to admissions staff

lesson_blocks.title: Step 1 — Inquiry Received
lesson_blocks.content: The workflow begins when a prospective student sends a course inquiry. This is the trigger that starts the process.

lesson_blocks.title: Step 2 — Capture Contact Details
lesson_blocks.content: The relevant contact details are captured so that the inquiry can be associated with the person who submitted it and handled through the workflow.

lesson_blocks.title: Step 3 — AI Identifies the Topic
lesson_blocks.content: AI is useful here because the inquiry may be written in natural language. The AI can examine the message and classify what the prospective student is asking about, such as course information, admissions, fees, or another topic.

lesson_blocks.title: Step 4 — Approved Course Information Retrieved
lesson_blocks.content: The workflow retrieves approved course information relevant to the identified topic. This is important because the response should be based on information the college has approved rather than relying on unsupported information.

lesson_blocks.title: Step 5 — Response Prepared
lesson_blocks.content: Using the inquiry and the approved information, a response can be prepared for the prospective student. AI may assist with language generation where appropriate.

lesson_blocks.title: Step 6 — Inquiry Logged
lesson_blocks.content: The inquiry is recorded so that the college has a record of the interaction. Logging can support follow-up, reporting, and management of inquiries.

lesson_blocks.title: Step 7 — Complex Requests Escalated
lesson_blocks.content: Complex requests are escalated to admissions staff. This keeps people involved when an inquiry requires additional judgment, authorization, account-specific handling, or information that the automated workflow should not provide on its own.

lesson_blocks.title: Why This Workflow Uses Both Automation and AI
lesson_blocks.content: Not every step requires AI. Capturing details, retrieving defined information, logging an inquiry, and routing work can often be handled through ordinary automation. AI becomes useful where the workflow needs capabilities such as understanding the inquiry, identifying its topic, or helping prepare a response.

lesson_blocks.title: Compare With Your Workflow
lesson_blocks.content: Compare your workflow with the model. Identify which steps in your design use simple automation, which steps genuinely benefit from AI, and which situations should be escalated to a person. Revise your workflow if you can make these responsibilities clearer.

title: Building AI Assistants
description: Learn what an AI assistant is and how to define its purpose, users, knowledge, boundaries, and human escalation requirements.

episodes.title: What Is an AI Assistant?
episodes.description: Learn what an AI assistant is and how to design one by defining its purpose, users, knowledge, boundaries, and escalation requirements.

lesson_blocks.title: What Is an AI Assistant?
lesson_blocks.content: An AI assistant is an AI-powered system designed to help users with defined tasks or information.

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding AI Assistants
lesson_blocks.content: An AI assistant is created for a particular purpose. Instead of expecting it to do everything, we define who it should help, what information it may use, what tasks it should support, what it must not do, and when a person should take over.

lesson_blocks.title: Examples of AI Assistants
lesson_blocks.content:
Examples include:

- Student information assistant
- Customer-service assistant
- Study assistant
- Employee support assistant
- Hotel guest assistant

lesson_blocks.title: The Five-Part Assistant Model
lesson_blocks.content:
1. PURPOSE — Why does it exist?

2. USERS — Who will use it?

3. KNOWLEDGE — What information can it use?

4. BOUNDARIES — What must it not do?

5. ESCALATION — When should a human take over?

lesson_blocks.title: 1. Purpose
lesson_blocks.content: Purpose answers the question: Why does the assistant exist? A clear purpose defines the problem the assistant is intended to help solve and prevents its role from becoming unnecessarily broad.

lesson_blocks.title: 2. Users
lesson_blocks.content: Users answers the question: Who will use the assistant? Knowing the intended users helps determine what kind of assistance they need and how the assistant should communicate with them.

lesson_blocks.title: 3. Knowledge
lesson_blocks.content: Knowledge answers the question: What information can the assistant use? The assistant should have access to information that is appropriate for its defined purpose, such as approved course information, company policies, service information, or other authorized knowledge.

lesson_blocks.title: 4. Boundaries
lesson_blocks.content: Boundaries answers the question: What must the assistant not do? Boundaries define limits on the assistant’s behavior. They help prevent the assistant from performing tasks, making claims, or providing information outside its permitted role.

lesson_blocks.title: 5. Escalation
lesson_blocks.content: Escalation answers the question: When should a human take over? Some requests may require human judgment, authorization, access, or handling. A well-designed assistant should recognize situations that need to be transferred to an appropriate person.

lesson_blocks.title: Putting the Five Parts Together
lesson_blocks.content: These five parts work together to define the assistant clearly. Purpose explains why it exists. Users identify who it serves. Knowledge defines what information it may use. Boundaries establish what it must not do. Escalation determines when responsibility should move to a person.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Define a Simple AI Assistant
lesson_blocks.content: Choose one AI assistant you could use in education, work, or business. Define its PURPOSE, USERS, KNOWLEDGE, BOUNDARIES, and ESCALATION. Keep the assistant focused on a clearly defined role rather than trying to make it perform every possible task.

lesson_blocks.title: Name
lesson_blocks.content: Hotel Guest Assistant

lesson_blocks.title: Purpose

lesson_blocks.title: Users

lesson_blocks.title: Knowledge

lesson_blocks.title: Can

lesson_blocks.title: Cannot

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Model
lesson_blocks.content: The assistant has a clearly defined role. It serves hotel guests using approved hotel information and can answer routine questions within that role. Its boundaries prevent it from inventing information, making unauthorized financial decisions, promising unavailable services, or overriding staff. Requests requiring additional authority or judgment are escalated to hotel staff.
