title: Building AI Agents
description: Learn what an AI agent is, how agents work toward defined goals through multiple steps, the basic components of an agent, and why permissions and human control are essential.

episodes.title: What Is an AI Agent?
episodes.description: Learn what an AI agent is and understand how an agent can work through multiple steps toward a defined goal using approved tools.

lesson_blocks.title: What Is an AI Agent?
lesson_blocks.content: At foundation level, an AI agent is a system designed to work toward a defined goal using multiple steps and, where permitted, approved tools.

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Definition
lesson_blocks.content: The important idea is that an AI agent can work toward a goal through a sequence of steps. Instead of only producing a response, an agent may need to understand a request, gather required information, use an approved system, take an allowed action, and check whether that action succeeded.

lesson_blocks.title: Simple Chatbot
lesson_blocks.content:
Question: “What time do you open?”

Answer: “We open at 9:00 AM.”

lesson_blocks.title: What Happens in the Simple Chatbot Example?
lesson_blocks.content: This is a straightforward question-and-answer interaction. The user asks for information and receives an answer. There is no need to complete a multi-step task such as checking availability, collecting a selection, creating a booking, or verifying that an action succeeded.

lesson_blocks.title: Agentic Task
lesson_blocks.content: “I would like to book an appointment Friday afternoon.”

lesson_blocks.title: Why This Is Different
lesson_blocks.content: Booking an appointment requires more than simply answering a question. The system has a goal to work toward and may need to complete several connected steps before that goal is achieved.

lesson_blocks.title: Possible Steps
lesson_blocks.content:
1. Understand request.
2. Identify date.
3. Identify preferred time.
4. Check approved calendar.
5. Present available options.
6. Receive selection.
7. Ask for confirmation.
8. Create appointment.
9. Verify success.
10. Send confirmation.

lesson_blocks.title: From Request to Result
lesson_blocks.content: Notice that the process does not jump directly from the customer request to creating an appointment. Information is identified, availability is checked, options are presented, the customer makes a selection, confirmation is requested, the appointment is created, and success is verified before confirmation is sent. This makes the process controlled and easier to check.

lesson_blocks.title: Approved Tools
lesson_blocks.content: The definition says an agent may use approved tools where permitted. A tool could be a system the agent is authorized to interact with in order to complete part of its task. In the appointment example, this could include an approved calendar or booking system. Access should be limited to what the agent actually needs for its defined role.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Identify the Steps
lesson_blocks.content: Imagine a customer asks an AI system to help schedule a service appointment. Write down the steps the system would need to complete from receiving the request to confirming the appointment. For each step, consider whether the system is only providing information or actually taking an action toward the goal.

episodes.title: Basic Agent Components
episodes.description: Learn the seven basic components used to define an AI agent: goal, instructions, information, tools, actions, checks, and escalation.

lesson_blocks.title: Basic Agent Components
lesson_blocks.content: An AI agent can be designed more clearly by defining the goal it should achieve, the rules it should follow, the information and tools it may use, the actions it may take, how success is checked, and when a human should take over.

lesson_blocks.title: 1. Goal
lesson_blocks.content:
GOAL: What should the system achieve?

The goal defines the result the agent is working toward. A clear goal helps keep the agent focused on a specific outcome rather than allowing it to act without a defined purpose.

lesson_blocks.title: 2. Instructions
lesson_blocks.content:
INSTRUCTIONS: What rules must it follow?

Instructions define how the agent should behave while working toward its goal. They may specify required steps, restrictions, organizational rules, or conditions the agent must follow.

lesson_blocks.title: 3. Information
lesson_blocks.content:
INFORMATION: What information may it use?

The agent needs appropriate information to complete its task. This should be information that is relevant and permitted for the agent's defined role.

lesson_blocks.title: 4. Tools
lesson_blocks.content:
TOOLS: Which systems can it access?

Tools are approved systems the agent may interact with when completing a task. For example, a booking agent may need authorized access to a reservation or calendar system. The agent should only receive access to tools necessary for its role.

lesson_blocks.title: 5. Actions
lesson_blocks.content:
ACTIONS: What actions may it take?

Actions define what the agent is permitted to do. Reading availability, creating an approved reservation, or sending a confirmation could be actions in a booking process. Clearly defining allowed actions helps prevent the agent from operating beyond its authority.

lesson_blocks.title: 6. Checks
lesson_blocks.content:
CHECKS: How does it verify success?

An agent should not simply assume that an action worked. Checks determine how the system confirms whether the intended result was actually achieved. For example, after creating a booking, the agent may need to verify that the booking was successfully recorded.

lesson_blocks.title: 7. Escalation
lesson_blocks.content:
ESCALATION: When does a human take over?

Not every situation should be handled automatically. Escalation defines the circumstances in which the agent should stop or transfer responsibility to a person, especially when human judgment, authority, or special handling is required.

lesson_blocks.title: How the Components Work Together
lesson_blocks.content: The goal tells the agent what outcome to work toward. Instructions define the rules. Information provides what it may know. Tools provide approved systems it may access. Actions define what it may do. Checks determine whether its actions succeeded. Escalation defines when responsibility must move to a human. Together, these components create a controlled structure for an AI agent.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Define an Agent
lesson_blocks.content:
Choose a simple agent you could use in education, work, or business. Define:

1. GOAL — What should it achieve?
2. INSTRUCTIONS — What rules should it follow?
3. INFORMATION — What information may it use?
4. TOOLS — Which systems may it access?
5. ACTIONS — What may it do?
6. CHECKS — How will it verify success?
7. ESCALATION — When should a human take over?

episodes.title: Human Control
episodes.description: Learn why AI agents require clear permission limits, appropriate human oversight, and escalation when decisions require additional authority or judgment.

lesson_blocks.title: Human Control
lesson_blocks.content: AI agents should not automatically receive unlimited authority. Permissions should be limited to what is necessary.

lesson_blocks.title: Why Permissions Matter
lesson_blocks.content: An AI agent may be able to interact with real systems and take actions. This makes permission control important. The agent should only receive the access and authority required to perform its defined role. Giving an agent more authority than necessary can increase the risk of incorrect, unauthorized, or unsuitable actions.

lesson_blocks.title: Limit Authority to the Task
lesson_blocks.content: The permissions given to an agent should match its responsibilities. For example, an agent that only needs to check appointment availability does not automatically need permission to change every calendar entry. An agent that provides customer information does not automatically need authority to approve financial transactions.

lesson_blocks.title: Scenario
lesson_blocks.content: Should a customer-service AI agent have unlimited refund authority?

lesson_blocks.title: Answer
lesson_blocks.content: No.

lesson_blocks.title: Why?
lesson_blocks.content: High-value or unusual refunds may require human authorization according to organizational rules.

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Scenario
lesson_blocks.content: A customer-service agent may be permitted to help collect refund information or handle certain routine cases, but this does not mean it should have unlimited authority. Organizations can define limits so that cases requiring greater financial authority, unusual judgment, or special approval are transferred to an authorized person.

lesson_blocks.title: Human Oversight and Escalation
lesson_blocks.content: Human control does not mean that every step must be performed manually. It means the organization decides which actions the agent may perform and which decisions remain under human authority. When the agent reaches a situation outside its permissions or defined boundaries, it should escalate the case rather than attempting to make an unauthorized decision.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Decide Where Human Control Is Needed
lesson_blocks.content: Imagine an AI agent is helping customers with orders. Identify three actions the agent could reasonably be allowed to perform and three situations that should require human authorization or escalation. Explain why you placed each action on that side of the boundary.

lesson_blocks.title: Unit 7 Model Answer
lesson_blocks.content: Compare the following model design with the Restaurant Reservation Agent you created in the Unit 7 assignment. Focus on whether your agent has a clear goal, collects the required information, uses an approved tool, follows a controlled workflow, verifies success, and escalates situations that require human involvement.

lesson_blocks.title: Goal
lesson_blocks.content: Help customers reserve tables.

lesson_blocks.title: Information Required
lesson_blocks.content:
The agent needs:

1. Date
2. Time
3. Number of guests
4. Customer name/contact details

lesson_blocks.title: Why This Information Is Required
lesson_blocks.content: The agent needs enough information to search for an appropriate reservation and identify the customer. Without the date, time, and number of guests, it cannot correctly check availability. The customer name and contact details allow the reservation to be associated with the person making the booking and support confirmation.

lesson_blocks.title: Tool
lesson_blocks.content: Authorized reservation system.

lesson_blocks.title: Why the Tool Must Be Authorized
lesson_blocks.content: The agent needs access to a reservation system to check availability and create the booking. That access should be approved and limited to the functions required for the reservation task. The agent should not automatically receive broader access or authority simply because it can use the system.

lesson_blocks.title: Workflow
lesson_blocks.content: Customer request → Collect required information → Check availability → Present options → Customer selects → Ask for confirmation → Create reservation → Verify success → Send confirmation

lesson_blocks.title: Understanding the Workflow
lesson_blocks.content: The workflow moves through controlled steps. The agent first receives the request and collects the information it needs. It then checks availability instead of inventing an available table. The customer is presented with options and makes a selection. Before the reservation is created, confirmation is requested. After creation, the agent verifies that the reservation succeeded before sending the final confirmation.

lesson_blocks.title: Escalation
lesson_blocks.content: Large groups, special events, complaints, or unusual requests go to restaurant staff.

lesson_blocks.title: Why Escalation Is Part of the Design
lesson_blocks.content: The agent is designed for a defined reservation task, not unlimited decision-making. Large groups, special events, complaints, and unusual requests may require judgment, additional authority, special arrangements, or organizational decisions. Escalating these cases keeps human control where it is needed.

lesson_blocks.title: Review Your Own Agent
lesson_blocks.content:
Compare your assignment with this model answer.

Check whether you clearly defined:

1. The agent's goal.
2. The information it must collect.
3. The approved tool it may use.
4. The sequence of actions it follows.
5. How it verifies that the reservation succeeded.
6. The situations that require human escalation.

Revise your design where necessary.

title: Problem Solving with AI
description: Learn how to begin with a real problem, determine whether AI is actually needed, and design practical AI-powered solutions with clear roles for AI, automation, human oversight, safeguards, and success measures.

episodes.title: Start With the Problem
episodes.description: Learn why practical AI solution design should begin by understanding the problem rather than immediately choosing AI, and introduce the complete problem-solving framework.

lesson_blocks.title: Start With the Problem
lesson_blocks.content:
Do not begin with:

“We need AI.”

Begin with:

WHAT PROBLEM ARE WE TRYING TO SOLVE?

lesson_blocks.title: Why the Problem Comes First
lesson_blocks.content: AI is a possible tool for solving a problem, but it should not automatically be the starting point. Before choosing AI, an organization or individual should first understand what is going wrong, who is affected, how the work is currently done, and what improvement is actually needed. Once the problem is clear, it becomes easier to decide whether AI, simple automation, another technology, a process change, or human action is appropriate.

lesson_blocks.title: Problem-Solving Framework
lesson_blocks.content: Problem → People → Current Process → Pain Point → Proposed Solution → AI Role → Automation Role → Human Role → Risks → Safeguards → Success Measures

lesson_blocks.title: 1. Problem
lesson_blocks.content: Clearly identify the problem that needs to be solved. Avoid beginning with a technology or product. Describe the actual situation that needs improvement.

lesson_blocks.title: 2. People
lesson_blocks.content: Identify the people affected by the problem. These may include customers, students, employees, managers, administrators, or other users. Understanding the people involved helps ensure that the proposed solution addresses a real need.

lesson_blocks.title: 3. Current Process
lesson_blocks.content: Understand how the task or process is handled today. Write down the existing steps before deciding how they should be changed. This helps reveal where delays, repetitive work, errors, or unnecessary manual effort occur.

lesson_blocks.title: 4. Pain Point
lesson_blocks.content: Identify the specific difficulty in the current process. A pain point could be slow response time, repetitive work, inconsistent information, high workload, frequent errors, or another problem that affects the people involved.

lesson_blocks.title: 5. Proposed Solution
lesson_blocks.content: Describe how the problem could be improved. At this stage, focus on the solution that is needed rather than assuming that every part must use AI.

lesson_blocks.title: 6. AI Role
lesson_blocks.content: If AI is useful, define exactly what AI should do. For example, AI might understand language, classify information, summarize text, generate a response, or identify patterns. The AI role should connect directly to the problem being solved.

lesson_blocks.title: 7. Automation Role
lesson_blocks.content: Define which repeatable process steps can happen automatically. Automation may move information between systems, record data, send notifications, trigger actions, or route work without requiring AI for every step.

lesson_blocks.title: 8. Human Role
lesson_blocks.content: Define what should remain under human responsibility. People may need to handle exceptions, sensitive decisions, approvals, complaints, disputes, or situations requiring judgment and authority.

lesson_blocks.title: 9. Risks
lesson_blocks.content: Consider what could go wrong. Depending on the solution, risks may include incorrect information, privacy problems, security issues, inappropriate actions, or decisions being made outside the intended boundaries.

lesson_blocks.title: 10. Safeguards
lesson_blocks.content: Define controls that reduce the identified risks. Safeguards may include approved information sources, permission limits, privacy controls, verification steps, human approval, and escalation procedures.

lesson_blocks.title: 11. Success Measures
lesson_blocks.content: Decide how you will know whether the solution is actually helping. Success should be measured against the original problem using appropriate measures such as response time, accuracy, user satisfaction, workload reduction, or other relevant results.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Start With a Problem
lesson_blocks.content:
Think of one real problem in education, work, or business. Do not start by saying that you need AI.

Work through the framework:

Problem → People → Current Process → Pain Point → Proposed Solution → AI Role → Automation Role → Human Role → Risks → Safeguards → Success Measures

If you reach the conclusion that AI is not necessary, that is also a valid solution-design decision.

episodes.title: Does the Problem Need AI?
episodes.description: Learn how to decide whether a problem actually requires Artificial Intelligence or can be solved more appropriately with simple automation or another straightforward solution.

lesson_blocks.title: Does the Problem Need AI?
lesson_blocks.content: After understanding a problem, the next question is whether Artificial Intelligence is actually necessary. Some problems can be solved effectively with simple rules, timers, traditional software, or automation. AI should be used when its capabilities are relevant to the problem.

lesson_blocks.title: Scenario 1
lesson_blocks.content: A business wants lights to switch on every evening at 6 PM.

lesson_blocks.title: Does This Require AI?
lesson_blocks.content: Answer: No.

lesson_blocks.title: Appropriate Solution
lesson_blocks.content: A timer or simple automation is sufficient.

lesson_blocks.title: Why AI Is Not Necessary
lesson_blocks.content: The requirement is predictable and follows a fixed rule: switch the lights on at a specific time. The system does not need to interpret language, classify information, generate content, identify patterns, or make a prediction. A simpler solution can perform the task directly.

lesson_blocks.title: Scenario 2
lesson_blocks.content: A company receives 20,000 customer comments and wants to identify major themes.

lesson_blocks.title: Could AI Help?
lesson_blocks.content: Answer: Yes, potentially. AI may help classify and summarize large amounts of unstructured text.

lesson_blocks.title: Why AI May Be Useful
lesson_blocks.content: Customer comments are written in natural language and may express the same idea in many different ways. Reviewing 20,000 comments manually could require substantial time and effort. AI may help analyze the text, group related comments into themes, and summarize recurring topics. The word potentially is important: the solution should still be evaluated for accuracy, privacy, cost, risks, and suitability.

lesson_blocks.title: Simple Automation or AI?
lesson_blocks.content:
A useful distinction is to ask what the task actually requires.

If the task follows clear, predictable rules, a simple automation may be enough.

If the task involves capabilities such as understanding large amounts of language, classifying unstructured information, summarizing content, generating responses, or identifying patterns, AI may be useful.

The objective is not to use the most advanced technology. The objective is to choose an appropriate solution for the problem.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Does It Need AI?
lesson_blocks.content:
For each problem below, decide whether you would begin with AI, simple automation, or another straightforward solution. Explain your reasoning.

1. Send employees a reminder every Friday at 4 PM.
2. Analyze thousands of open-ended customer reviews to identify recurring complaints.
3. Automatically save every submitted website form into a database.
4. Summarize a large collection of written support messages into major themes.

For each case, focus on what the problem requires rather than assuming that AI must be used.

episodes.title: AI Solution Design
episodes.description: Learn a practical 12-question framework for designing an AI-powered solution, covering the problem, users, current process, pain points, AI and automation roles, human control, data, risks, safeguards, and success measures.

lesson_blocks.title: AI Solution Design
lesson_blocks.content: Use these 12 questions.

lesson_blocks.title: 1. What problem exists?
lesson_blocks.content:
Example Answer: Students wait too long for answers to common enrollment questions.

Start by defining the actual problem. This keeps the solution focused on a real need rather than starting with a technology.

lesson_blocks.title: 2. Who is affected?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: Prospective students and admissions staff.

Identify the people who experience the problem or are involved in the process. A useful solution should consider the needs of the people it affects.

lesson_blocks.title: 3. What happens today?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: Staff manually answer each inquiry.

Understanding the current process shows how the work is being performed before a new solution is introduced.

lesson_blocks.title: 4. What are the pain points?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: Slow response, repetitive work, and inconsistent answers.

Pain points identify the specific weaknesses in the current process that the proposed solution should improve.

lesson_blocks.title: 5. What is the proposed solution?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: An AI-powered student information assistant.

The proposed solution should respond directly to the problem and pain points already identified.

lesson_blocks.title: 6. What will AI do?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: Understand questions, identify topics, retrieve approved information, and generate clear responses.

Define the AI role precisely. This prevents AI from being added without a clear purpose and makes it easier to determine which capabilities are actually required.

lesson_blocks.title: 7. What will automation do?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: Log inquiries, retrieve information, send routine responses, and route requests.

AI and automation are related but not identical. Automation can handle predictable process steps while AI handles tasks that benefit from capabilities such as language understanding or generation.

lesson_blocks.title: 8. What remains under human control?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: Complaints, disputes, exceptions, and sensitive decisions.

Clearly defining the human role prevents the system from receiving unlimited authority. Situations requiring judgment, special authorization, or sensitive decision-making can remain with people.

lesson_blocks.title: 9. What data is needed?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: Courses, schedules, approved fees, FAQs, and necessary contact information.

Identify the information required for the solution to work. The information should be relevant, appropriate, and handled according to applicable privacy and security requirements.

lesson_blocks.title: 10. What could go wrong?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: Incorrect answers, privacy issues, or unauthorized commitments.

Thinking about possible failures before deployment helps identify where controls and safeguards are required.

lesson_blocks.title: 11. What safeguards are needed?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: Approved information sources, permission limits, privacy controls, and human escalation.

Safeguards reduce the risks identified in the previous question. They define how the solution will be controlled and how situations outside its boundaries will be handled.

lesson_blocks.title: 12. How will success be measured?
lesson_blocks.content:
Answer: Response time, accuracy, satisfaction, workload reduction, and escalation rates.

Success measures help determine whether the solution actually improves the original problem. A solution should be evaluated by results, not simply by whether AI was implemented.

lesson_blocks.title: Putting the 12 Questions Together
lesson_blocks.content: The questions form a complete solution-design process. First understand the problem, people, current process, and pain points. Then define the proposed solution and separate the roles of AI, automation, and humans. Finally identify the required data, possible risks, safeguards, and measurable indicators of success.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice — Design an AI Solution
lesson_blocks.content:
Choose one real problem in education, work, or business and answer all 12 questions:

1. What problem exists?
2. Who is affected?
3. What happens today?
4. What are the pain points?
5. What is the proposed solution?
6. What will AI do?
7. What will automation do?
8. What remains under human control?
9. What data is needed?
10. What could go wrong?
11. What safeguards are needed?
12. How will success be measured?

Your answers should describe one connected solution rather than twelve unrelated ideas.

episodes.description: Study a complete sample capstone project showing how a practical AI-powered solution can be structured from the problem and users through workflow, human oversight, risks, safeguards, benefits, and success measures.

lesson_blocks.title: Complete Sample Capstone Project
lesson_blocks.content: AI-POWERED STUDENT INFORMATION ASSISTANT

lesson_blocks.title: 1. Problem
lesson_blocks.content:
A training institution receives many repeated questions every day about:

• Courses
• Fees
• Schedules
• Online learning
• Enrollment
• Office location

Staff repeatedly answer the same questions.

lesson_blocks.title: 2. Users
lesson_blocks.content:
• Prospective students
• Current students
• Admissions staff

lesson_blocks.title: 3. Current Process
lesson_blocks.content:
Student sends message
↓
Staff reads message
↓
Staff identifies question
↓
Staff searches for information
↓
Staff responds
↓
Student asks another question
↓
Staff responds again

lesson_blocks.title: 4. Pain Points
lesson_blocks.content:
• Slow responses
• Repetitive staff work
• Inconsistent answers
• High staff workload
• Delays during busy periods

lesson_blocks.title: 5. Proposed Solution
lesson_blocks.content: Develop an AI-powered Student Information Assistant.

lesson_blocks.title: 6. AI Role
lesson_blocks.content:
The AI can:

• Understand student questions
• Identify the inquiry topic
• Retrieve approved information
• Generate clear responses
• Handle basic follow-up questions
• Identify cases that need staff help

lesson_blocks.title: 7. Automation Role
lesson_blocks.content:
Inquiry received
↓
Question classified
↓
Approved information retrieved
↓
Response generated
↓
Interaction recorded
↓
Complex request escalated

lesson_blocks.title: 8. Workflow
lesson_blocks.content:
STUDENT MESSAGE
↓
AI UNDERSTANDS REQUEST
↓
APPROVED INFORMATION RETRIEVED
↓
RESPONSE GENERATED
↓
RESPONSE SENT
↓
HUMAN ESCALATION IF NEEDED

lesson_blocks.title: 9. Human Role
lesson_blocks.content:
Human staff remain responsible for:

• Admission decisions
• Complaints
• Payment disputes
• Sensitive cases
• Policy exceptions
• Final decisions requiring authority

lesson_blocks.title: 10. Risk 1 — Incorrect Information
lesson_blocks.content: Safeguard: Use approved institutional information and escalate uncertain cases.

lesson_blocks.title: 11. Risk 2 — Privacy
lesson_blocks.content: Safeguard: Collect only necessary data, use approved systems, and restrict access.

lesson_blocks.title: 12. Risk 3 — Unauthorized Promises
lesson_blocks.content: Safeguard: Create clear boundaries and prevent the AI from making commitments outside its authority.

lesson_blocks.title: 13. Benefits
lesson_blocks.content:
Potential benefits include:

• Faster responses
• More consistent information
• Reduced repetitive work
• Better availability
• More staff time for complex cases

lesson_blocks.title: 14. Success Measures
lesson_blocks.content:
Measure:

• Average response time
• Accuracy
• Student satisfaction
• Number of inquiries handled
• Escalation rate
• Staff time saved

lesson_blocks.title: Compare With Your Capstone
lesson_blocks.content: Compare your own Final Capstone Project with this complete sample. Check whether your problem, users, current process, pain points, proposed solution, AI role, automation role, workflow, human oversight, risks, safeguards, benefits, and success measures form one clear and practical solution. Revise your project where necessary.

episodes.title: Sample Capstone Presentation
episodes.description: Study the coursebook sample showing how a learner can present a practical AI capstone project clearly and concisely.

lesson_blocks.title: Sample Capstone Presentation Answer
lesson_blocks.content: The following is the sample capstone presentation answer provided in the coursebook. Use it to understand how the main parts of a project can be communicated clearly in a short presentation.

lesson_blocks.title: Opening
lesson_blocks.content: Good morning.

lesson_blocks.title: Project Introduction
lesson_blocks.content: My project is called the AI-Powered Student Information Assistant.

lesson_blocks.title: Problem
lesson_blocks.content: The problem I identified is that educational institutions receive many repetitive questions about courses, fees, schedules, and enrollment.

lesson_blocks.title: Current Challenge
lesson_blocks.content: Staff spend significant time answering the same questions.

lesson_blocks.title: Proposed Solution
lesson_blocks.content: My proposed solution is an AI-powered assistant that understands student questions, retrieves approved institutional information, and provides clear responses.

lesson_blocks.title: Human Oversight
lesson_blocks.content: The AI does not replace admissions staff. Routine inquiries can be handled automatically, while complex, sensitive, or unusual cases are escalated to staff.

lesson_blocks.title: Expected Benefits
lesson_blocks.content: The expected benefits include faster responses, consistent information, and reduced repetitive workload.

lesson_blocks.title: Success Measures
lesson_blocks.content: Success can be measured using response time, accuracy, student satisfaction, escalation rates, and staff time saved.

lesson_blocks.title: Closing
lesson_blocks.content: Thank you.

lesson_blocks.title: Practice Your Presentation
lesson_blocks.content: Using your own capstone project, prepare a short presentation following the same general flow: introduce your project, explain the problem, describe the current challenge, present your proposed solution, explain the role of human oversight, state the expected benefits, identify how success will be measured, and close the presentation clearly.

questions.question: Define Generative AI.
questions.correct_answer: AI capable of generating new content such as text, images, audio, video, or code based on input.

questions.question: What is a workflow?
questions.correct_answer: A sequence of connected steps used to complete a task or process.

questions.question: What is an AI assistant?
questions.correct_answer: An AI-powered system designed to help users with defined tasks or information.

questions.question: What is an AI agent?
questions.correct_answer: An AI-powered system designed to work through multiple steps toward a defined goal and potentially interact with approved tools.

questions.question: Why is human oversight important?
questions.correct_answer: Because AI may make mistakes, misunderstand context, exceed intended boundaries, or encounter decisions requiring human judgment and authority.
